title: Lighter Than Air: France and England, 1783–1785
subtitle: The first balloon flights, from Annonay and Paris to London and the Channel, 1782–1785
intro: In the eighteen months between June 1783 and January 1785 people went from watching a paper globe rise over a market town in the Vivarais to crossing the sea by air. The idea, the first trials and a kind of mastery all fall inside two years, and they happened in public, before kings, crowds of tens of thousands, and some of the most careful letter-writers of the age.

Two methods raced each other. The Montgolfier brothers, papermakers from Annonay, filled their envelopes with smoke and heated air; the physicist Jacques Charles and the Robert brothers used the 'inflammable air' (hydrogen) that chemists had only lately learned to make. Within weeks of each other, Paris saw an unmanned hydrogen globe vanish into cloud, a sheep, a duck and a cockerel go up before Louis XVI, men lifted on a rope in a wallpaper maker's garden, and finally two men carried freely across the city.

The honest record here is mostly letters and published accounts rather than diaries. Benjamin Franklin, American minister at Passy, watched several of the ascents and wrote long letters about them to Joseph Banks at the Royal Society; Banks's replies show London moving from wonder to caution. Faujas de Saint-Fond turned the experiments into a book almost as they happened. The aeronauts themselves — d'Arlandes, Charles, Lunardi, Jeffries — wrote accounts for publication, which makes them vivid and self-interested at once.

Some of the people who mattered most left almost nothing. The villagers of Gonesse, who attacked the first hydrogen globe as a monster, appear only through the government's notice telling the public not to be afraid. James Sadler, the Oxford pastry cook who became the first English aeronaut, wrote nothing; what survives is what reporters set down. Pilâtre de Rozier, the first man to fly, is seen through procès-verbaux, newspapers and his companions.

The chapter crosses to England in 1784, when Lunardi, Sadler and Blanchard made the first ascents there and Horace Walpole mocked the craze, and ends with the Channel crossing of Blanchard and Jeffries in January 1785. Its coda is sober: in June 1785 Pilâtre de Rozier and Pierre Romain were killed trying to cross the other way, the first deaths in the air.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian (New Style): France had used the Gregorian calendar since 1582 and Britain since 1752. Franklin's letter headed 'Nov. 21' was written 22–25 November 1783, and Walpole's letter headed 15 October 1784 describes a balloon usually dated 16 October; the entries give the date of the event or of writing as noted.

eyes.name: Joseph-Michel Montgolfier
eyes.role: Papermaker's son from Annonay, aged 42 in 1782; restless self-taught experimenter, twelfth of sixteen children
eyes.side: France; the Montgolfier paper mills of Annonay (Vivarais)
eyes.vantage_label: the inventor at home in the provinces
eyes.form: dated letters and family papers (edited by Gillispie); official procès-verbal
eyes.authenticity: The brothers' letters survive in family and museum collections and were used at length by C. C. Gillispie, The Montgolfier Brothers and the Invention of Aviation (1983). The Annonay launch is attested by the procès-verbal of the États particuliers du Vivarais and by Faujas's published account. Joseph's own early letter to Étienne is known in translation; its exact day is not fixed.
eyes.bio: The dreamer of the pair, he watched heated air lift a small taffeta box in his lodgings at Avignon and wrote to his brother at once. He stayed largely in the south while Étienne carried the invention to Paris, so his vantage is the origin and the provinces, not the court.

sources.title: Linda Hall Library, Scientist of the Day: the Montgolfier brothers

eyes.name: Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier
eyes.role: Manager of the family paper business, aged 38 in 1783; the brother sent to Paris to demonstrate the machine
eyes.side: France; Montgolfier firm, working with the wallpaper maker Jean-Baptiste Réveillon
eyes.where: Paris (Réveillon's works, faubourg Saint-Antoine) and Versailles
eyes.form: dated letters (to his brother and his wife); memoir read to the Académie
eyes.authenticity: His letters from Paris are held in Montgolfier family papers and quoted by Gillispie (1983) and later historians; the letter to his wife on the Versailles launch is cited as written the evening after the event. His memoir read to the Académie royale des sciences on 6 March 1784 is printed in Faujas, vol. 1.
eyes.bio: Practical, anxious and deeply invested, Étienne had to turn his brother's discovery into a royal spectacle with borrowed workshops and the weather against him. His letters record the business of invention: a balloon wrecked by rain, a king touring the preparations, a rival using the new gas.

sources.title: Château de Versailles: first hot-air balloon flight

eyes.name: Jacques-Alexandre-César Charles
eyes.role: Physicist and popular lecturer in Paris, aged 37; built the hydrogen balloon with the Robert brothers, instrument makers
eyes.side: France; the Paris scientific public and the subscription organised by Faujas
eyes.where: Champ de Mars and the Tuileries, Paris
eyes.vantage_label: the rival inventor, in the basket
eyes.form: published account of his ascent and contemporary reports
eyes.authenticity: Charles's own narrative of 1 December 1783 was printed in the press and in the literature of 1783–84 (Faujas's Première suite covers the flight); the figures below follow standard modern summaries of these accounts.
eyes.bio: Charles chose the 'inflammable air' that Cavendish had described rather than the Montgolfiers' smoke, and so built the ancestor of every gas balloon. His December flight with the younger Robert brother was the first carefully instrumented ascent; then, alone at sunset, he went higher, saw the sun again, and never flew afterwards.

sources.title: Science History Institute, 'Artificial Clouds and Inflammable Air'

eyes.name: Benjamin Franklin
eyes.role: American minister plenipotentiary to France, aged 77; living at Passy; Fellow of the Royal Society
eyes.where: Passy, on the western edge of Paris, a short walk from La Muette
eyes.vantage_label: foreign envoy and eyewitness, writing to London
eyes.authenticity: The letters to Joseph Banks survive and are edited with full notes in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin (Founders Online). The letter headed 'Nov. 21' was actually written 22–25 November, as the editors show. The 'new-born baby' remark appears in none of Franklin's own letters; it was recorded by Grimm's Correspondance littéraire and repeated in altered forms, and its authenticity is debated.
eyes.bio: Franklin was the best-placed foreign witness: an old natural philosopher with a carriage, a pocket glass and a correspondent at the head of the Royal Society. His letters to Banks are precise, sceptical about rumour, worried for the men in the gallery, and quick to imagine uses.

eyes.name: Sir Joseph Banks
eyes.role: President of the Royal Society, aged 40; naturalist of Cook's first voyage
eyes.where: London, and his Lincolnshire estate during the summer recess
eyes.authenticity: His replies to Franklin survive and are edited in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin (Founders Online), with notes drawing on Charles Blagden's letters to him.
eyes.bio: Banks received the French news first-hand from Franklin and had to decide how the Royal Society should respond. His letters swing from exhilaration in September to institutional caution in November, ending with a wry division of the spoils between 'practical' French and 'theoretical' English flight.

eyes.name: Barthélemy Faujas de Saint-Fond
eyes.role: Geologist and assistant naturalist at the Jardin du Roi, aged 42; organiser of the public subscription for Charles's balloon
eyes.authenticity: Description des expériences de la machine aérostatique de MM. de Montgolfier (Paris: Cuchet, 1783) and Première suite (1784), the first full-length account of the experiments; the second volume includes Charles's December flight and a commission report dated 23 December 1783. The first volume was reissued with a short supplement on the first free flight.
eyes.bio: Faujas turned the experiments into a book almost as they happened, gathering procès-verbaux, letters and measurements. He was a partisan organiser as well as a recorder, so his figures carry the enthusiasm of the subscription he ran.

sources.title: History of Information: Faujas reports on the first aerial voyages

eyes.name: Jean-Charles-Pierre Lenoir
eyes.role: Lieutenant-général de police of Paris, aged 51; co-signed the public notice on balloons with the intendant Bertier de Sauvigny
eyes.where: Paris; the notice was aimed at country people such as those of Gonesse
eyes.vantage_label: the state, answering the villagers' fear
eyes.authenticity: The 'Avertissement au peuple' is a printed government notice dated Paris, 27 August 1783, signed De Sauvigny and Lenoir; an English translation is reproduced in E. C. Vivian, A History of Aeronautics. The villagers of Gonesse left no words of their own; their reaction survives only through this notice, prints and the savants' reports.
eyes.bio: The Gonesse villagers who met Charles's globe are among the chapter's most vivid presences and its least recorded: no name or sentence of theirs survives. The police lieutenant's notice is the official trace of their encounter, and the first attempt by a state to tell the public what an aircraft is.

sources.title: Vivian, A History of Aeronautics, Appendix C (translation of the notice)

eyes.name: Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier
eyes.role: Physicist and keeper of a natural-history cabinet for the king's brother; founder of a Paris museum (1781); aged 29
eyes.where: Réveillon's garden, La Muette, Versailles, Boulogne-sur-Mer
eyes.form: procès-verbaux, press notices and others' accounts (no diary)
eyes.authenticity: Pilâtre left no diary; his ascents are recorded in procès-verbaux signed by witnesses, in the Journal de Paris and other papers, in Faujas, and in Franklin's letters. His death is known from contemporary reports of witnesses at Boulogne.
eyes.bio: Ambitious and publicity-minded, Pilâtre volunteered to go up before the Academy thought it safe, made the first tethered ascents in October 1783, and then the first free flight in November. He died eighteen months later trying to cross the Channel from France, in the first fatal air accident.

sources.title: Le Roy to Franklin [19 Oct 1783?], with notes on the tethered trials

eyes.name: François Laurent, marquis d'Arlandes
eyes.role: Infantry officer, aged 41; Pilâtre's companion on the first free flight
eyes.where: In the gallery of the Montgolfier balloon over Paris
eyes.authenticity: D'Arlandes wrote a lively account of the flight in a letter printed in the literature of 1784 (commonly cited as addressed to Faujas); its exact date is not confirmed here. The official procès-verbal of the flight was signed by witnesses; Franklin enclosed a copy to Banks.
eyes.bio: A soldier with a sense of comedy, d'Arlandes recorded the flight from inside: the sparks burning holes in the envelope, the wet sponge, and his partner calling for more fire. He went to see Franklin the same evening.

sources.title: Linda Hall Library, Scientist of the Day: François Laurent d'Arlandes

eyes.name: Vincenzo (Vincent) Lunardi
eyes.role: Secretary to the Neapolitan ambassador in London, in his twenties
eyes.where: Artillery Ground, Moorfields, London, to Hertfordshire
eyes.form: published letters (An Account of the First Aërial Voyage in England, 1784)
eyes.authenticity: An Account of the First Aërial Voyage in England (London: John Bell, 1784) is a compilation of his letters to his guardian Gherardo Compagni, with newspaper reports and illustrations; written for publication and self-promoting.
eyes.bio: Lunardi brought ballooning to London as theatre, with a paying crowd, the Prince of Wales, and a cat, a dog and a pigeon in the car. His letters are a performer's, but they record the first flight over England in the flier's own words.

sources.title: Science History Institute: An Account of the First Aërial Voyage in England (1784)
Wonders of World Aviation: Tytler and Lunardi

eyes.name: James Sadler
eyes.role: Oxford pastry cook in the family shop, aged about 31; self-taught chemist
eyes.form: press reports of his statements (no writings of his own)
eyes.authenticity: Sadler wrote no books or journals; his 1784 flights are known from Oxford newspaper reports and later studies (J. E. Hodgson, 'James Sadler of Oxford', Trans. Newcomen Society, 1927–28).
eyes.bio: The first English-born aeronaut was a cook, not a gentleman of the Royal Society. He is a reminder that the record keeps the showmen and the savants better than the craftsmen: what survives of Sadler is what reporters wrote down after he landed.

sources.title: Oxford: James Sadler and other balloon ascents, 4 Oct 1784

eyes.name: Jean-Pierre Blanchard
eyes.role: French inventor and professional aeronaut, aged 31
eyes.authenticity: His letter to Franklin of 16 November 1784 is edited in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin. He also issued printed accounts of his voyages; those are not used directly here.
eyes.bio: Blanchard was the first to make flying a career, charging patrons for seats. His rivalry with his paying passenger Jeffries at Dover is one of the great quarrels of early aviation, and the Channel crossing was his.

sources.title: British Balloon Museum & Library: Jean-Pierre Blanchard

eyes.name: Dr John Jeffries
eyes.role: Boston-born physician (Harvard 1763), Loyalist living in London, aged 39; paying passenger and scientific observer
eyes.vantage_label: the passenger who paid for the voyage
eyes.authenticity: Jeffries kept a diary (unpublished, Harvard) and published A Narrative of the Two Aerial Voyages of Doctor Jeffries with Mons. Blanchard (London, 1786); two signed manuscripts of the Narrative are at Houghton Library.
eyes.bio: Jeffries paid 100 guineas for a seat and brought barometer and thermometer to make the flight scientific. His account is the passenger's: the bargaining, the cold, the slow sinking toward the sea, and everything thrown overboard to stay up.

sources.title: Harvard Magazine, 'Dr. Jeffries balloons across the Channel' (2021)
William Franklin to W. T. Franklin, 16 Dec 1784, with notes on Jeffries

eyes.name: Horace Walpole
eyes.role: Man of letters and collector, aged 66; prolific letter-writer
eyes.where: Berkeley Square, London, and Strawberry Hill, Twickenham
eyes.vantage_label: the ironic onlooker of the mania
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Sir Horace Mann and H. S. Conway, printed in the nineteenth-century editions and in the Yale Edition of Horace Walpole's Correspondence; the texts here follow the Project Gutenberg selection.
eyes.bio: Walpole watched balloon mania as a social phenomenon: fashion moving into the air, senators and ladies talking of nothing else. Once, in October 1784, his servants called him out to see one pass.

sources.title: Letters of Horace Walpole, vol. II (Project Gutenberg)

entries.headline: A taffeta box rises to the ceiling
entries.digest: In lodgings at Avignon, Joseph built a small box of thin wood and taffeta, held a flame beneath it, and watched it lift off its stand and strike the ceiling. He wrote to Étienne urging him to lay in taffeta and cordage quickly, promising to show him something astonishing. The letter is known from family papers in translation and its day is not fixed.
entries.source_note: Gillispie (1983) as summarised in 'Montgolfier brothers' overview; month only.

entries.headline: The paper globe before the Estates of Vivarais
entries.digest: The brothers inflated a globe of cloth and paper, about 800 cubic metres and buttoned together, over a fire before the assembled États particuliers du Vivarais. It rose out of sight for about ten minutes and came down some two kilometres away; the height was estimated at well over a thousand metres. A procès-verbal was drawn up and the news was carried to Paris, where the Academy invited a repeat.
entries.source_note: Faujas, Description (1783); Annonay procès-verbal; figures from Gillispie as summarised in overview; 'aec n136' article (anciensmeteos.info).

entries.headline: 'Of what use is a new-born baby?' — a reported quip
entries.digest: Asked what use a balloon was, Franklin is said to have answered by asking the use of a new-born baby. The remark is recorded not in his letters but in Grimm's Correspondance littéraire, and spread in altered forms; the editors of his papers think Grimm's version Franklinian, while S. L. Chapin judged it a legendary embellishment.
entries.source_note: Founders Online 01-40-02-0342, headnote and footnote on the quip (Grimm; Chapin).

entries.headline: The first hydrogen globe goes up in the rain
entries.digest: Charles and the Robert brothers had filled a small rubberised-silk globe with hydrogen from iron and acid and moved it by night to the Champ de Mars. At about five in the afternoon, at a cannon signal, it was released before a huge crowd and climbed into cloud. About three-quarters of an hour later it came down near Gonesse, some 21 km away, where it was destroyed.
entries.source_note: Franklin to Banks 30 Aug 1783 (time, signal); figures from standard summaries (Jacques Charles overview).

entries.headline: Fifty thousand watch a globe vanish
entries.digest: Franklin described the globe as twelve feet across, of varnished silk, filled with 'inflammable air' and able to lift 39 pounds beyond its own weight. He counted not less than 50,000 people, watched it shrink as it rose, and saw it enter the clouds. The crowd went home delighted, trading wild ideas for its use.
entries.source_note: Franklin to Banks, 30 Aug–2 Sept 1783, Founders Online 01-40-02-0342.

entries.headline: The subscription's organiser describes a sublime moment
entries.digest: Faujas, who had raised the public subscription that paid for the globe, wrote of the crowd's emotion as it rose, finding the sight admirable and sublime. His account became the first printed narrative of the launch.
entries.source_note: Faujas, Description (1783), as cited in Science History Institute, 'Artificial Clouds and Inflammable Air'.

entries.headline: A notice to the public: do not be afraid
entries.digest: The intendant Bertier de Sauvigny and the police lieutenant Lenoir issued a printed notice explaining that globes of heated air or 'inflammable air' had been sent up at Annonay and Paris, that more were planned, and that anyone seeing one in the sky should know it was harmless and might one day serve society. It followed the destruction of Charles's globe by frightened country people at Gonesse, whose own words were not recorded.
entries.source_note: Notice dated Paris, 27 August 1783, signed De Sauvigny and Lenoir; translation in Vivian, History of Aeronautics, App. C. Printing and posting date not confirmed.

entries.headline: Postscript: the villagers took it for an animal
entries.digest: Adding to his letter, Franklin reported that the globe had taken about 150 seconds to reach the clouds, at about 500 toises. The country people who saw it land thought it a living creature because it bounced, and attacked it with stones and knives. He added that Pilâtre had asked the Academy for leave to go up and been told to wait.
entries.source_note: Franklin to Banks, 30 Aug–2 Sept 1783, postscript; Founders Online 01-40-02-0342.

entries.headline: Rain ruins the balloon meant for the king
entries.digest: Étienne had built a large decorated balloon at Réveillon's wallpaper works for a trial before the Academy commissioners. After a test on 11 September, storms and rain on the 12th destroyed it, and a new one had to be made in days for the royal demonstration.
entries.source_note: Founders Online notes to Le Roy [19 Oct 1783?] ('the one destroyed on Sept. 12'); Gillispie as summarised in overview; Étienne's letters not seen directly.

entries.headline: A road into the air
entries.digest: Before the Society's caution set in, Banks wrote that the present day was an epoch: the balloon had opened a road into the air, comparable to the invention of shipping. He imagined balloons as counterpoises lightening carriages, and planned to send one up as an electrical kite.
entries.source_note: Banks to Franklin, 13 Sept 1783, Founders Online 01-40-02-0397.

entries.headline: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel before the king
entries.digest: At about one o'clock, before Louis XVI, the royal family and a vast crowd, the balloon Le Réveillon rose from Versailles carrying a sheep, a duck and a cockerel in a basket. It stayed up about eight minutes and came down in the wood of Vaucresson. Writing to his wife that evening, Étienne described the royal family touring the preparations.
entries.source_note: Château de Versailles, key dates (time, landing); Lewis Theobald, Lumen 39 (2020), on Étienne's letter to his wife written the evening after.

entries.headline: Measuring the royal launch
entries.digest: Faujas noted that by noon the palace courtyards and windows were packed. The balloon, 57 feet high and 41 across, rose, hung, and descended slowly about eight minutes later some 1,700 toises away at the Maréchal crossroads in the wood of Vaucresson. He denied reports that the cockerel had been hurt, blaming a scrape on a kick from the sheep.
entries.source_note: Faujas, Description, vol. 1, pp. 36–40, as cited by Lewis Theobald, Lumen 39 (2020).

entries.headline: Not at Versailles, but sending the prints
entries.digest: Franklin admitted he had not been at Versailles but passed on what he was told: the balloon filled in about ten minutes over burning straw, rose about 200 toises and came down as the air cooled, and only the cock was hurt. He described the duc de Crillon's illuminated balloon, aloft about eleven and a half hours, and said he meant to subscribe to Charles's planned balloon for a man.
entries.source_note: Franklin to Banks, 8 Oct 1783, Founders Online 01-41-02-0053.

entries.headline: First man off the ground, on a rope
entries.digest: In Réveillon's small courtyard, before principals and scientists, Pilâtre went up in the gallery of a tethered Montgolfier balloon, feeding a fire slung beneath it, to the length of the ropes, roughly a hundred feet by later reckoning. Others were lifted a few feet the same afternoon. Pilâtre's own publicity afterwards brought crowds to the next trials.
entries.source_note: BBML 'Who was the first to fly?' (Dollfus; Courier d'Avignon); Founders Online notes to 01-41-02-0087. Heights vary between accounts.

entries.headline: The inventor tests his own machine
entries.digest: Several accounts, drawing on Étienne's own text and the press, record that he too rose on the tether during these trials; some modern accounts place his ascent before Pilâtre's on the same day. The family and the publicist thus left rival claims to the first human ascent.
entries.source_note: Montgolfier brothers overview (Gillispie, 'most likely' 15 Oct); BBML citing Courier d'Avignon (dateline 18 Oct).

entries.headline: Four ascents and nine minutes at 324 feet
entries.digest: Before more than two thousand spectators Pilâtre went up four times, twice with a companion, climbing and descending at will by feeding the fire. On the last ascent he held the balloon at 324 feet for at least nine minutes.
entries.source_note: Founders Online, notes to Le Roy to Franklin [19 Oct 1783?], 01-41-02-0087.

entries.headline: Franklin's balloon letters read to the Fellows
entries.digest: Banks read Franklin's two papers on aerostatic machines to the Royal Society, and the Fellows were pleased to see him back at philosophy. Writing next day, Banks offered to print them in the Philosophical Transactions, but said the more respectable Fellows were wary of 'Ballomania' and wanted a balloon to carry a useful experiment before backing mere height.
entries.source_note: Banks to Franklin, 7 Nov 1783, Founders Online 01-41-02-0128.

entries.place: Above Paris, from La Muette to the Butte-aux-Cailles
entries.headline: Sparks, a wet sponge and a shout for more fire
entries.digest: Launched from the garden of La Muette in the early afternoon, d'Arlandes and Pilâtre stood on opposite sides of the gallery, unable to see each other except through gaps. D'Arlandes, watching Paris and the river, was called to keep feeding the fire; he found sparks burning small holes in the envelope and put them out with a wet sponge. They crossed the Seine and came down after about 25 minutes between two windmills.
entries.source_note: Linda Hall Library, d'Arlandes; Ministère des Armées, '21 novembre 1783'. D'Arlandes's printed letter account not seen directly.

entries.headline: The first free flight
entries.digest: Pilâtre and d'Arlandes made the first untethered human flight, about 25 minutes and some 9 km, rising perhaps 900 m over the Invalides and the Tuileries before landing beyond the city wall. A procès-verbal was signed by witnesses on the spot.
entries.source_note: Ministère des Armées, '21 novembre 1783'; Franklin to Banks 22–25 Nov 1783 (procès-verbal enclosed).

entries.place: Garden of La Muette, near Passy
entries.headline: Anxious for the men in the gallery
entries.digest: Franklin watched from the garden of La Muette among the gentry, fearing the men might be thrown out or burned as the gallery caught in treetops at the start. That evening d'Arlandes and Montgolfier called at his house. Writing over the next days, he enclosed the procès-verbal and reported that they had come down gently without the least shock.
entries.quote: lit gently without the least Shock
entries.source_note: Franklin to Banks headed 'Nov. 21' [i.e., 22–25 Nov 1783], Founders Online 01-41-02-0148.

entries.headline: Charles's grand balloon deferred
entries.digest: Franklin wrote that the hydrogen balloon of Charles and the Roberts was delayed till the next day because filling it had taken longer than expected. He enclosed newspapers containing the journal of the first aerial voyage made by men and promised a report.
entries.source_note: Franklin to Banks, 30 Nov 1783, Founders Online 01-41-02-0164.

entries.headline: Two hours over the Île-de-France with instruments
entries.digest: At about a quarter to two Charles and the younger Robert brother rose from the Tuileries in a hydrogen balloon with valve, net and sand ballast, after a small pilot balloon was released to test the wind. With barometer and thermometer they flew about two hours and covered some 36 km, landing near Nesles-la-Vallée, where riders led by the duc de Chartres caught them.
entries.source_note: Jacques Charles overview; Franklin to Banks 1–2 Dec 1783 notes (younger Robert); BnF print record naming Marie-Noël Robert.

entries.headline: Alone, a second sunset, and never again
entries.digest: With Robert out of the car the lightened balloon shot upward, by his estimate to about 3,000 m. Charles saw the sun again after it had set on the ground, felt sharp dry cold and a pain in his ear, valved gas, and came down about 3 km away. He did not fly again.
entries.source_note: Jacques Charles overview; Science History Institute article (Charles's account quoted on the cold).

entries.place: His carriage near the statue of Louis XV
entries.headline: Watching through a pocket glass
entries.digest: Slightly unwell, Franklin stayed in his carriage near the statue of Louis XV rather than entering the Tuileries. He described an infinite crowd at windows and on roofs, the balloon rising perhaps 300 toises, the travellers waving a white pennant, and himself following it with his glass until it seemed no bigger than a walnut.
entries.source_note: Franklin to Banks, 1–2 Dec 1783, Founders Online 01-41-02-0167.

entries.headline: Fashion has gone up into the air
entries.digest: Writing to Mann in Florence beside news of Fox's India Bill, Walpole mocked the craze: everyone's eyes were turned to the air, and he, late in life, found people staring at the idea of a voyage to the moon.
entries.quote: Balloons occupy senators, philosophers, ladies, everybody.
entries.source_note: Walpole to Mann, 2 Dec 1783, Letters (Gutenberg vol. II).

entries.headline: Practical flying to France, theory to England
entries.digest: Banks judged Charles's hydrogen flight decisive and thought it should be repeated in England at full scale, recalling Wilkins and Cavendish as English forerunners. He thought it foolish to fight over credit already won, and proposed to concede practical flying to the French while claiming the theory for the English.
entries.source_note: Banks to Franklin, 9 Dec 1783, Founders Online 01-41-02-0182.

entries.headline: Joseph's own flight in Le Flesselles
entries.digest: At Lyon a very large hot-air balloon, Le Flesselles, went up with several passengers including Joseph and Pilâtre, and came down roughly after a short flight. It is the only ascent Joseph is known to have made.
entries.source_note: Montgolfier brothers overview (Gillispie pp. 92–93, 'early 1784'); exact day and passenger list not checked.

entries.headline: Blanchard's first ascent
entries.digest: Blanchard, who had been building 'flying vessels' since 1782, made his first balloon ascent from the Champ de Mars with a hydrogen balloon fitted with wings or oars meant to steer it. The Franklin editors call an early March test unsuccessful; the steering devices did not work.
entries.source_note: BBML biography (March 1784); Founders Online notes to 01-43-02-0176. Day commonly given as 2 March, not confirmed.

entries.headline: The inventor reports to the Academy
entries.digest: Étienne's memoir on the machine was read to the Academy, setting out the brothers' account of the invention and its trials. It was printed in Faujas's first volume.
entries.source_note: Lewis Theobald, Lumen 39 (2020), citing Faujas vol. 1, pp. 287–95.

entries.headline: Above the clouds with Proust
entries.digest: Before Louis XVI and Gustav III of Sweden, Pilâtre and the chemist Joseph Proust rose in the large Montgolfier balloon La Marie-Antoinette. They climbed above the clouds to perhaps 3,000 m and travelled about 52 km in some 45 minutes before cold forced them down near Luzarches.
entries.source_note: Pilâtre de Rozier overview; figures are estimates.

entries.headline: The Prince of Wales watches him go
entries.digest: With a huge paying crowd growing restless and his balloon not fully filled, Lunardi left his friend George Biggin behind and went up alone shortly before one o'clock, with a dog, a cat and a pigeon. Statesmen and the Prince of Wales watched him drift northward over the city.
entries.source_note: Science History Institute record of the Account (1784); Wonders of World Aviation; Lunardi overview.

entries.place: North Mymms and Standon Green End, Hertfordshire
entries.headline: Putting the cat down, then landing at Standon
entries.digest: Lunardi briefly came down in a field at North Mymms to set ashore the cat, which had become unwell, then rose again and finally landed at Standon Green End near Ware, about 24 miles from London after some two and a quarter hours.
entries.source_note: Science History Institute record (24 miles, Standon Green End); Wonders of World Aviation (duration).

entries.headline: An Oxford cook flies six miles
entries.digest: Sadler went up in a hot-air balloon of his own making, fed by a stove in the car, and reached about 3,600 feet by his barometer. He came down near Woodeaton, some six miles away, and told reporters that the height caused no trouble beyond being colder than the ground.
entries.source_note: James Sadler overview (Hodgson 1927–28); Oxford local history page on 4 Oct 1784.

entries.headline: Called out by the servants to see a balloon
entries.digest: In the middle of a letter to Conway, Walpole's servants called him outside to see a balloon pass, which he supposed to be Blanchard's, due to be let off from Chelsea. He mused ironically on balloons replacing ships. Blanchard's Chelsea ascent with John Sheldon is dated 16 October, so the letter may have been finished a day after its heading.
entries.quote: my servants called me away to see a balloon
entries.source_note: Walpole to Conway, Strawberry Hill, 15 Oct 1784 (Gutenberg vol. II); date of Blanchard's ascent from Founders Online notes.

entries.headline: A paying passenger from the Royal Society
entries.digest: Blanchard made his first English ascent from Chelsea, taking up for a fee John Sheldon, a surgeon and Fellow of the Royal Society. It began his practice of selling seats to patrons that would put Jeffries in his car.
entries.source_note: Founders Online notes to Blanchard to Franklin, 16 Nov 1784.

entries.headline: Hydrogen this time
entries.digest: Sadler flew a hydrogen-filled balloon from Oxford, reaching the neighbourhood of Aylesbury after about twenty minutes, again recorded only through reports of others.
entries.source_note: James Sadler overview.

entries.headline: Writing to Franklin before the sea crossing
entries.digest: Blanchard told Franklin he meant to cross the Channel before the month was out, starting from Dover Castle with the court's permission, and hoped the wind would carry him to Paris or even Versailles. He complained of satires against him in the Paris papers and said Franklin's approval mattered more.
entries.source_note: Blanchard to Franklin, 16 Nov 1784, Founders Online 01-43-02-0176.

entries.headline: The doctor's first flight
entries.digest: Having agreed on 6 November to pay Blanchard 100 guineas for a joint voyage, Jeffries went up with him from London and came down in Kent, taking readings with his instruments. It was the first of the two voyages his Narrative describes.
entries.source_note: Founders Online notes to Blanchard to Franklin, 16 Nov 1784; Jeffries, Narrative (1786).

entries.headline: Carrying a letter across the sea
entries.digest: On the eve of leaving for Dover, Jeffries accepted a letter from William Franklin to his son in Passy, who wished to be among the first to receive a letter carried across the Channel by air. The pair reached Dover on 18 December and waited about three weeks for a wind.
entries.source_note: William Franklin to W. T. Franklin, 16 Dec 1784, Founders Online 01-43-02-0237, with notes.

entries.headline: Throwing out everything, even their clothes
entries.digest: After quarrels at Dover in which Blanchard tried to keep him out of the car, Jeffries rose with him from the cliffs at about one. Within the hour they were sinking toward the sea and threw out ballast, provisions, equipment, a wing, and then their clothes. About five miles off France the balloon rose again, and they came down before four in the forest of Guînes, where local people brought them clothing.
entries.source_note: Founders Online notes to 01-43-02-0237; Harvard Magazine (2021); Jeffries, Narrative (1786).

entries.place: Dover Castle to the forest of Guînes
entries.headline: The Channel crossed by air
entries.digest: Blanchard's balloon, about 27 feet across, made the first crossing of the sea by air, in about two and a half hours. Both men were fêted in France; Jeffries was received at Versailles the following week.
entries.source_note: This Day in Aviation (Jeffries tag) for times and size; Founders Online notes to 01-43-02-0237 for Versailles. Blanchard's own printed account not seen directly.

entries.headline: At Franklin's table
entries.digest: Jeffries reached Paris, sent on William Franklin's letter to his son, and that evening called on Benjamin Franklin at Passy, where he dined several times over the following month before leaving on 21 February.
entries.source_note: Founders Online notes to 01-43-02-0237 (citing Jeffries's diary).

entries.headline: The first fatal air accident
entries.digest: Attempting to cross the Channel from France in a combined hydrogen and hot-air balloon, Pilâtre and his companion Pierre Romain rose from Boulogne early in the morning. About half an hour later, carried back over the coast by a change of wind, the envelope failed, reportedly catching fire and deflating, and both men fell near Wimereux, about 5 km from the start. A monument now marks the place.
entries.source_note: Pilâtre de Rozier overview; 'aec n136' article; contemporary accounts as summarised there.

entries.headline: Balloons and Herschel's worlds
entries.digest: Writing to Mann after the season of ascents and deaths, Walpole joked that the arts might wait until balloons improved enough to carry them to the millions of worlds Herschel was discovering.
entries.quote: by the improvement of balloons they may be transported
entries.source_note: Walpole to Mann, 30 Oct 1785, Letters (Gutenberg vol. II).

claims.claim: Heated air lifts a small taffeta box to the ceiling at Avignon; the idea of the balloon
claims.evidence: Joseph's letter to Étienne (family papers, Gillispie 1983)

claims.claim: First public balloon launch, Annonay: ~800 m³ paper-and-cloth globe, ~10 minutes aloft, ~2 km travelled, height estimated 1,600–2,000 m
claims.evidence: Procès-verbal of the États particuliers du Vivarais; Faujas (1783)

claims.claim: First hydrogen balloon (12 ft diameter, unmanned): ~150 s to the clouds at ~500 toises; ~45 minutes; down at Gonesse ~21 km away and destroyed by villagers
claims.evidence: Franklin to Banks 30 Aug–2 Sept 1783; Faujas; avertissement of 27 Aug

claims.claim: Sheep, duck and cockerel flown at Versailles: ~8 minutes, landed ~1,700 toises (~3.5 km) away in the wood of Vaucresson; all three survive
claims.evidence: Faujas, Description vol. 1, pp. 36–40; Franklin 8 Oct 1783 (~200 toises height, hearsay)

claims.claim: First human ascent, tethered, at Réveillon's: Pilâtre to the rope's length (~80–100 ft); a rival position holds that Étienne Montgolfier went up first that day
claims.evidence: Faujas; Courier d'Avignon (dateline 18 Oct); Dollfus; Gillispie

claims.claim: Tethered ascents before 2,000+: four ascents, height of 324 ft held for at least 9 minutes
claims.evidence: Papers of Benjamin Franklin, notes to Le Roy [19 Oct 1783?]

claims.claim: First free human flight, La Muette to the Butte-aux-Cailles: ~25 minutes, ~9 km, ~900 m
claims.evidence: Procès-verbal signed by witnesses (copy sent by Franklin to Banks); d'Arlandes's letter account

claims.claim: First manned hydrogen flight, Tuileries to Nesles-la-Vallée: ~2 h 5 min, ~36 km; then Charles alone to ~3,000 m
claims.evidence: Charles's published account; Franklin to Banks 1–2 Dec 1783

claims.claim: Academy commission (with Lavoisier) reports on the aerostatic machines; printed in Faujas's Première suite (1784), pp. 200–231
Pilâtre and Proust in La Marie-Antoinette: ~52 km in ~45 minutes, ~3,000 m, landing near Luzarches
claims.evidence: Contemporary reports as summarised in modern accounts

claims.claim: First aerial voyage in England: Artillery Ground to Standon Green End, ~24 miles in ~2¼ hours. Position: James Tytler's short hot-air 'leaps' at Edinburgh (25 Aug 1784, some sources 27 Aug) came first in Britain
claims.evidence: Lunardi, Account (1784); Tytler from Edinburgh press as summarised by aviation historians

claims.claim: First English-born aeronaut: Oxford to Woodeaton, ~6 miles, ~3,600 ft by barometer
claims.evidence: Oxford press reports; Hodgson, Trans. Newcomen Soc. (1927–28)

claims.claim: First crossing of the sea by air, Dover Castle to the forest of Guînes: ~1 p.m. to before 4 p.m., about 2½ hours, nearly everything jettisoned
claims.evidence: Jeffries, Narrative (1786) and diary; Papers of Benjamin Franklin notes

claims.claim: Pilâtre de Rozier and Pierre Romain killed when their combined hydrogen and hot-air balloon failed about half an hour after leaving Boulogne; fell near Wimereux

convergences.label: The first hydrogen globe, Champ de Mars to Gonesse
convergences.note: The builder records the gas and the lift, Franklin the crowd and the orange-sized speck, Faujas the sublime, and the police the problem: country people who met the thing at Gonesse attacked it, and the state had to explain to everyone what a flying machine was.

convergences.label: Animals before the king at Versailles
convergences.note: Étienne writes as the anxious exhibitor, Faujas as the measurer, and Franklin, who was not there, passes on hearsay and a print, a reminder of how much of the record is second-hand.

convergences.label: Men go up on a rope in Réveillon's garden
convergences.note: Two claims to be first off the ground sit side by side: the publicist's and the inventor's family's, both resting on the same handful of reports.

convergences.label: The first free flight from La Muette
convergences.note: From inside the gallery, the flight is sparks and shouting; from the garden, it is a dangerous lurch into treetops and a long anxious watch. The two views meet at Franklin's house that evening.

convergences.label: Charles and Robert rise from the Tuileries
convergences.note: Charles is above the clouds with his thermometer, Franklin in his carriage with a pocket glass; in London Walpole mocks the mania the next day, and within the week Banks concedes 'practical' flight to France.

convergences.label: The Royal Society hears the news
convergences.note: Franklin's letters are read to the Fellows, and the institution's caution about 'Ballomania' meets the enthusiasm of its president's September letter.

convergences.label: England's first autumn of flight
convergences.note: Within five weeks an Italian showman, an Oxford cook and a French professional all go up, and Walpole is called out of doors by his servants to see one pass.

convergences.label: The Channel crossed by air
convergences.note: The passenger's narrative is of quarrels, cold and sinking toward the sea; the pilot's triumph is national; four days later the American Loyalist doctor is dining with the American minister at Passy.

ties.note: Franklin's letters from Passy were Banks's main source on the French flights, and Banks read them to the Royal Society on 6 November 1783.
D'Arlandes and Montgolfier called on Franklin on the evening of the first free flight, 21 November 1783.
Jeffries visited and dined with Franklin at Passy after the Channel crossing, carrying a letter from Franklin's estranged Loyalist son William.
Blanchard wrote to Franklin from London on 16 November 1784 announcing the Channel attempt and seeking his approval.
Paying passenger and professional pilot: partners in the air, adversaries at Dover, where Blanchard tried to keep Jeffries out of the car.
Brothers and partners; Joseph's idea, Étienne's Parisian demonstrations.
Companions in the gallery on 21 November 1783, on opposite sides of the fire.
Pilâtre flew Étienne's tethered balloon at Réveillon's in October 1783; their accounts leave rival claims to the first ascent.
Hydrogen against hot air: Charles's globe repeated the Montgolfier experiment with a different gas, and the two methods competed through the autumn of 1783.
Faujas organised the public subscription that paid for Charles's first globe and then chronicled both rival methods.
The police notice of 27 August 1783 explained Charles's globe to a public frightened by its landing at Gonesse.
Walpole supposed the balloon he was called out to see in October 1784 was Blanchard's from Chelsea.
Lunardi met Sadler, the first English aeronaut, at Oxford in July 1785.

threads_out.note: Franklin left Passy in July 1785, weeks after Pilâtre's death, and was back in Philadelphia that September; two years later he sat in the Constitutional Convention there. His balloon letters to Banks are among the last scientific writing of his French mission.

Lavoisier, who sat on the Academy's 1783 balloon commission, was guillotined in 1794, and the revolutionary army formed a company of aérostiers whose observation balloon flew at Fleurus that year; Réveillon's wallpaper works, where the October 1783 ascents were made, was sacked in the riot of April 1789.

Charles's December 1783 balloon, with its valve, net and ballast, set the pattern for gas envelopes, and Blanchard's wings and oars were early attempts to steer one: the problem the airship builders took up.
Blanchard and Jeffries's crossing from Dover to Guînes in January 1785 was the first flight over the strait that heavier-than-air machines would cross in 1909.
Joseph Banks, who received Franklin's balloon letters as President of the Royal Society, had been the naturalist of Cook's Endeavour voyage of 1768–71.
